name: Petit Paquet
description: Petit Paquet (also known as 'Turkish Packets' or 'Paquets Turcs') is an 18th-century French game of pure chance and high-stakes gambling. It pits a single 'Banker' against a group of players. The game is played with several small piles (packets) of face-down cards. Players bet on specific piles, and the top cards are revealed one by one. It is a precursor to modern casino games like Baccarat and Pharaoh, known for its elegant simplicity and rapid wealth transfer.

history.origins: Dates back to the royal courts of France in the 1700s. It was particularly popular during the 'Turkish Fad' (Turquerie) in Europe, hence the alternative name.
timeline: 1710s: First described in French gaming manuals as a parlor gamble.
1850s: Becomes a staple in common gambling dens across Paris and London.
1920s: Mostly replaced in casinos by Baccarat, but remains a folk game in Rural France.
Present: Played occasionally as a historical curiosity or in high-stakes private circles.
history.cultural: Symbolizes the 'Golden Age' of French salon gambling, where fortunes were won and lost on the flip of a single 'Paquet'.
history.evolution: The game evolved from a 32-card format (removing low cards to increase the 'Hit' frequency) to a full 52-card format for more participants.

setup.players: One Banker and any number of Punters (Players).
setup.dealing: The Banker splits the deck into several small face-down packets (usually 5 to 10 piles) and one 'Banker Pile' for themselves.

rules.objective: Bet on a packet that reveals a higher card than the Banker's card.
rules.gameplay: The Banker splits the deck into several face-down packets (typically 5 to 10) and keeps one Banker pile. Punters place bets on one or more packets. The top card of each packet and the Banker pile is revealed. Each punter wins if their chosen packet's top card ranks higher than the Banker's card; Banker wins ties. Winnings are paid out; then a new round may begin.
keyRules: Banker wins all ties. Punters bet on which packet will show a higher card than the Banker's card. Spread bets across packets to manage risk. Banker must have sufficient bankroll to cover all punter wins.

strategy.basic: In a game of pure chance, there is no mathematical way to 'Win' Petit Paquet, but there is a way to 'Manage Losses'. Spread your bets! Never put all your tokens on a single packet. If you spread across three packets, you only need one card to be higher than the Banker's to potentially break even (depending on house rules for ties).
strategy.intermediate: The 'Banker's Fatigue': Watch the deck. If many Aces and Kings have already been revealed in the first few rounds of a deck, the Banker's pile is statistically more likely to turn up lower cards in the late-game. This is when you should increase your bets on the Punters' side.
strategy.advanced: Banker Management: The Banker has a massive statistical advantage because they win on all 'Ties'. If you have the opportunity to serve as Banker, take it! However, you must have enough capital (the 'Bankroll') to pay out simultaneously if all 10 packets reveal higher cards than yours. A Banker with a small bankroll is easily 'Broken'.
tips: This is a 'Sucker Game' in professional settingsâ€”the house edge is significant. Play it for the social tension and the historical flavor rather than profit.
If playing with a 32-card deck, the Aces and 10s appear much more frequently, leading to a much more volatile game.
